AL.summary: Yes. Alabama courts still treat the smell of marijuana by itself as probable cause to search you and your car, even though legal hemp smells the same.
AL.inPractice: In Bain v. State (2024), the Court of Criminal Appeals upheld an odor-only search despite hemp legalization, saying it is bound by Alabama Supreme Court precedent (Adams v. State, 2001).

sources.label: Bain v. State, No. CR-2024-0321 (Ala. Crim. App. Sept. 27, 2024)

AK.summary: Unclear. Marijuana is legal for adults in Alaska, and we found no Alaska appellate ruling since legalization on whether odor alone justifies a car search.
AK.inPractice: Older Alaska cases let odor count toward suspicion or probable cause, but all predate legalization. A 2021 legal survey found no newer ruling, and we could not confirm one since.

sources.label: Marijuana Policy Project / Perkins Coie, 2021 State Analysis Chart (Alaska)
State v. Smith (Alaska Ct. App. 2008)

AZ.summary: No. Arizona law says the odor of marijuana or burnt marijuana does not by itself even create reasonable suspicion of a crime, which is a lower bar than probable cause.
AZ.inPractice: The rule, A.R.S. § 36-2852(C) from 2020's Prop 207, doesn't apply when an officer is investigating impaired driving. Odor can still be combined with other facts.

AR.summary: Yes. Arkansas courts have long held that the smell of marijuana from a lawfully stopped car is enough probable cause to search it and its occupants.
AR.inPractice: A 2024 Court of Appeals case (Whiting v. State) relied on the rule, though that search also involved a dog alert and erratic driving. We found no ruling on whether medical marijuana or hemp changes it.

sources.label: Brunson v. State (Ark. 1997)
Whiting v. State, 2024 Ark. App. 176

CA.summary: No. Since Prop 64, California courts have held that the smell of marijuana, or a small legal amount in the car, isn't enough by itself to search your vehicle.
CA.inPractice: In People v. Johnson (2020), odor plus a small amount of marijuana didn't justify a search. Signs of impaired driving, an open container, or occupants under 21 can change the result.

sources.label: People v. Johnson, No. C089373 (Cal. Ct. App. 2020)
Cal. Health & Safety Code § 11362.1(c)

CO.summary: Unclear. Colorado's Supreme Court says marijuana odor can count toward probable cause, but it has never squarely decided whether odor alone is enough since legalization.
CO.inPractice: People v. Zuniga (2016) found probable cause from odor plus other facts. People v. McKnight (2019) held a sniff by a marijuana-trained dog is itself a search that needs probable cause.

sources.label: People v. Zuniga, 2016 CO 52
People v. McKnight, 2019 CO 36
StreetSense: Colorado marijuana odor and car searches (Oct. 2026)

CT.summary: No. Connecticut law says the odor of cannabis or burnt cannabis can't be probable cause or reasonable suspicion for a stop or search, and evidence found that way can't be used in court.
CT.inPractice: Under § 54-33p, officers may still use odor when testing a driver they reasonably suspect is impaired. Police groups pushed in 2025 to loosen the rule; we found no change to it.

sources.label: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 54-33p

DE.summary: Unclear. Before legalization, Delaware's Supreme Court let odor support a car search. Adult use became legal in 2023, and we found no ruling on how that changes things.
DE.inPractice: Juliano v. State (2021) held odor alone can't justify an arrest, though it can be one factor toward probable cause to search. Fowler v. State (2016) upheld an odor-based car search.

sources.label: Juliano v. State (Del. 2021)
Fowler v. State (Del. 2016)

DC.summary: No. D.C. law says the odor of marijuana or burnt marijuana isn't even reasonable suspicion of a crime, so it can't by itself justify a search.
DC.inPractice: D.C. Code § 48-921.02a (2014) doesn't apply when police are investigating impaired driving. Other facts, like evidence of more than an ounce, can still matter.
DC.detail: Possession legal since 2015; no retail sales

FL.summary: Generally no. Two Florida appeals courts, ruling en banc in 2024 and 2025, held that the smell of cannabis alone no longer gives probable cause to search a car.
FL.inPractice: Baxter (5th DCA, 2024) and Williams (2d DCA, 2025, overruling Owens) treat odor as one factor. Other districts haven't squarely decided; we found no Florida Supreme Court ruling.

sources.label: Baxter v. State, 389 So. 3d 803 (Fla. 5th DCA 2024) (en banc)
Williams v. State, No. 2D2023-2200 (Fla. 2d DCA Oct. 1, 2025) (en banc)
Pumphrey Law: What every Florida appeals court says (Oct. 2025)

GA.summary: Yes. Georgia courts still treat the smell of marijuana coming from a car as probable cause to search it, despite legal hemp.
GA.inPractice: In Gowen v. State (2021), the Court of Appeals rejected the argument that officers must be able to tell marijuana from hemp by smell before relying on the odor.

sources.label: Gowen v. State, No. A21A0651 (Ga. Ct. App. 2021)

HI.summary: Unclear. We found no Hawaii appellate ruling on whether marijuana odor alone justifies a car search. Hawaii has medical marijuana and has decriminalized very small amounts.
HI.inPractice: A 1980 Hawaii Supreme Court case (State v. Dorson) said odor "may establish probable cause." A 2021 legal survey found no vehicle case on point; we could not confirm newer rulings.
HI.detail: Medical only; up to 3 g decriminalized

sources.label: Marijuana Policy Project / Perkins Coie, 2021 State Analysis Chart (Hawaii)

ID.summary: Yes. Idaho courts have held that the smell of marijuana alone can be probable cause to search a car's passenger area.
ID.inPractice: Idaho cases say burnt-marijuana odor alone doesn't justify searching the trunk, while raw-marijuana odor may (State v. Gonzales, 1990). We found no ruling on whether legal hemp changes this.

sources.label: Marijuana Policy Project / Perkins Coie, 2021 State Analysis Chart (Idaho)

IL.summary: It depends on the type. Illinois' Supreme Court says burnt cannabis odor alone isn't enough to search your car, but raw cannabis odor alone is, because cannabis must ride in a sealed, odor-proof container.
IL.inPractice: People v. Redmond (2024) covers burnt odor; People v. Molina (2024) covers raw odor, relying on the container rule in 625 ILCS 5/11-502.15. We label this "unsettled" because the rule splits.

sources.label: People v. Redmond, 2024 IL 129201
People v. Molina, 2024 IL 129237
State Court Report: legalization and search-and-seizure law (2025)

IN.summary: Yes. Indiana's Court of Appeals held in 2023 that an officer smelling marijuana from a car has probable cause to search it, even though legal hemp smells the same.
IN.inPractice: In Moore v. State (Ind. Ct. App. 2023), the court said odor that could be hemp or marijuana still showed a "fair probability" of contraband. We found no Indiana Supreme Court ruling on the hemp issue.

sources.label: Moore v. State, 211 N.E.3d 574 (Ind. Ct. App. 2023), as quoted in Bain v. State (Ala. Crim. App. 2024)

IA.summary: Probably yes. Marijuana isn't legal in Iowa, and we found nothing showing Iowa has moved away from treating marijuana odor as probable cause. We could not confirm a current ruling.
IA.inPractice: We did not verify a recent Iowa appellate decision on odor, including whether legal hemp changes the analysis. Treat this entry as unconfirmed.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Legality of cannabis by U.S. jurisdiction (legal status only)

KS.summary: Probably yes. Marijuana is fully illegal in Kansas, and we found nothing showing Kansas has moved away from treating marijuana odor as probable cause. We could not confirm a current ruling.
KS.inPractice: We did not verify a recent Kansas appellate decision on odor, including whether legal hemp changes the analysis. Treat this entry as unconfirmed.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Cannabis in Kansas (legal status only)

KY.summary: Probably yes. Recreational marijuana isn't legal in Kentucky, and we found nothing showing courts have stopped treating odor as probable cause. We could not confirm a current ruling.
KY.inPractice: We did not verify a recent Kentucky appellate decision on odor, or how the state's medical cannabis law (passed 2023) or legal hemp affects it. Treat this entry as unconfirmed.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Legality of cannabis by U.S. jurisdiction (legal status only)

LA.summary: Probably yes, but unconfirmed. Louisiana allows medical marijuana and made possession of 14 grams or less a fine-only offense in 2021, but recreational use is still illegal.
LA.inPractice: We could not confirm whether Louisiana courts have changed the traditional odor rule in light of medical flower, decriminalization, or legal hemp. Treat this entry as unconfirmed.
LA.detail: Medical only; up to 14 g decriminalized

sources.label: Wikipedia: Cannabis in Louisiana (legal status only)

ME.summary: Unclear. Marijuana is legal for adults in Maine, and a 2021 legal survey found no Maine court ruling on whether odor alone justifies a search. We found none since.
ME.inPractice: The same survey reported an anecdotal account of an officer not searching after being reminded marijuana is legal. We could not confirm any official police policy.

sources.label: Marijuana Policy Project / Perkins Coie, 2021 State Analysis Chart (Maine)

MD.summary: No. Since July 2023, Maryland law says police can't start a stop or search based only on the smell of burnt or unburnt cannabis. Evidence found that way is inadmissible, even with consent.
MD.inPractice: Under Crim. Proc. § 1-211, if police are investigating cannabis-impaired driving, they may search only areas the driver can readily reach or that likely hold evidence of impairment.

sources.label: Md. Code, Crim. Proc. § 1-211

MA.summary: No. Massachusetts' highest court has held that the smell of burnt marijuana (2011) or unburnt marijuana (2014) alone doesn't justify a car search.
MA.inPractice: Commonwealth v. Cruz (2011) and Commonwealth v. Overmyer (2014) came after decriminalization and before 2016 legalization. Odor can still be weighed with other evidence.

sources.label: Commonwealth v. Overmyer, SJC-11481 (Mass. 2014)
Commonwealth v. Overmyer (opinion text)

MI.summary: No. Michigan's Supreme Court ruled in 2025 that, since legalization, the smell of marijuana alone isn't probable cause to search a car, overruling its own 2000 decision.
MI.inPractice: People v. Armstrong (2025) says odor can still be one factor, such as with signs a driver is intoxicated. A July 2026 ruling (People v. Wilkins) reportedly limited searches for civil infractions.

sources.label: People v. Armstrong, No. 165233 (Mich. Apr. 2, 2025)
ThisIsWhyImHigh: car searches and weed smell by state (Oct. 2026; Wilkins summary)

MN.summary: No. Minnesota's Supreme Court held in 2023 that odor alone isn't probable cause to search a car, and a 2024 law says odor can't be the sole basis to search a vehicle or its occupants.
MN.inPractice: State v. Torgerson (Minn. 2023) treats odor as one factor among the totality of circumstances. Minn. Stat. § 626.223 now puts that rule in statute.

sources.label: Minn. Stat. § 626.223
State v. Torgerson, 995 N.W.2d 164 (Minn. 2023)

MS.summary: Yes. Mississippi courts have held that if an officer clearly smells marijuana, that can be probable cause to search the vehicle and its passengers.
MS.inPractice: These rulings (e.g., Boches v. State) predate Mississippi's 2022 medical marijuana law. We found no decision on whether medical use or hemp changes the rule.

sources.label: Marijuana Policy Project / Perkins Coie, 2021 State Analysis Chart (Mississippi)

MO.summary: No. Missouri's constitution, amended in 2022, says the odor of marijuana is not reasonable suspicion of a crime, so it can't by itself justify a search.
MO.inPractice: The rule in Article XIV, § 2 doesn't apply when police are investigating whether a driver is under the influence of marijuana.

sources.label: Mo. Const. art. XIV, § 2

MT.summary: No. Montana's Supreme Court has said odor alone is closer to suspicion than probable cause, and Montana's legalization law says legal marijuana activity can't be a basis to search adults 21+.
MT.inPractice: State v. Schoendaller (1978); Mont. Code § 16-12-106. Montana has no general automobile exception, so car searches need more. Impaired driving or use while driving isn't protected.

sources.label: Marijuana Policy Project / Perkins Coie, 2021 State Analysis Chart (Montana)

NE.summary: Yes. Nebraska's Supreme Court held in 2018 that the odor of marijuana alone gives probable cause to search a vehicle, despite legalization in neighboring states.
NE.inPractice: State v. Seckinger (2018) reaffirmed decades of Nebraska precedent. Voters approved medical marijuana in 2024; we found no ruling on whether that changes the odor rule.
NE.detail: Not legal; medical approved by voters 2024

sources.label: Marijuana Policy Project / Perkins Coie, 2021 State Analysis Chart (Nebraska, discussing State v. Seckinger)

NV.summary: Unclear. Marijuana is legal for adults in Nevada, and the cases treating odor as probable cause came before legalization. We found no Nevada appellate ruling since.
NV.inPractice: A 2021 survey reported Nevada Highway Patrol said troopers try to develop other indicators for adults but search without more if the person is under 21. We couldn't confirm current policy.

sources.label: Marijuana Policy Project / Perkins Coie, 2021 State Analysis Chart (Nevada)

NH.summary: Probably no. New Hampshire's Supreme Court rejected the idea that marijuana odor alone automatically creates even reasonable suspicion, which is a lower bar than probable cause.
NH.inPractice: State v. Perez (2020) treats odor as one factor in the totality of circumstances. It addressed suspicion to extend a stop, not a car search directly. Small amounts are decriminalized.

sources.label: Marijuana Policy Project / Perkins Coie, 2021 State Analysis Chart (New Hampshire)
Baxter v. State (Fla. 5th DCA 2024), citing State v. Perez, 239 A.3d 975 (N.H. 2020)

NJ.summary: No. Under New Jersey's 2021 legalization laws, the odor of marijuana, burnt or raw, by itself is not reasonable suspicion to stop or search you.
NJ.inPractice: The Attorney General's 2021 reference card tells officers this. For people under 21, odor also isn't probable cause to search their vehicle for underage-possession violations.

sources.label: N.J. Attorney General, Marijuana Reference Card (updated Mar. 26, 2021)

NM.summary: No. New Mexico's Cannabis Regulation Act says the odor of cannabis or burnt cannabis is not reasonable suspicion of a crime and not a basis to stop, detain, or search you.
NM.inPractice: The rule (NMSA § 26-2C-25) doesn't apply when an officer is investigating whether you're driving while intoxicated or impaired.

sources.label: Cannabis Regulation Act, HB 2 (N.M. 2021 Spec. Sess.)

NY.summary: No. New York's 2021 cannabis law says the smell of cannabis or burnt cannabis can't, on its own, be the basis for finding reasonable cause to believe a crime was committed.
NY.inPractice: Penal Law § 222.05. In impaired-driving investigations, burnt-cannabis odor may be considered, but it can't justify searching areas the driver can't readily reach.

sources.label: N.Y. Penal Law § 222.05

NC.summary: Yes. North Carolina's Court of Appeals has repeatedly held that the odor of marijuana alone is still probable cause to search a vehicle, even though legal hemp smells the same.
NC.inPractice: State v. Dobson, State v. Little, and State v. Rowdy (all 2024). Review petitions were pending at the N.C. Supreme Court in 2025; we could not confirm whether it has ruled.

sources.label: UNC School of Government: Spring 2025 Cannabis Update
UNC School of Government: Criminal Law Case Update (June 2025)

ND.summary: Probably yes. North Dakota cases say the smell of marijuana may establish probable cause, but they predate the state's 2019 decriminalization, and we found no newer ruling.
ND.inPractice: State v. Schmalz (2008) is one example. In a later case (In re K.V.), the court found car odor wasn't enough to search a passenger. Treat the current rule as unconfirmed.

sources.label: Marijuana Policy Project / Perkins Coie, 2021 State Analysis Chart (North Dakota)

OH.summary: Unsettled. Ohio's Supreme Court said in 2000 that odor alone is probable cause, but since 2023 legalization, Ohio appeals courts have split on whether that still holds.
OH.inPractice: State v. Gray (1st Dist. 2025) said odor alone isn't enough; State v. Dejournett (9th Dist. 2026) upheld a burnt-odor search since smoking in a car is illegal. The Ohio Supreme Court hasn't ruled.

sources.label: State v. Gray, 2025-Ohio-4607 (1st Dist.)
State v. Dejournett, 2026-Ohio-640 (9th Dist.)

OK.summary: Probably yes, but unconfirmed. Oklahoma allows only licensed medical marijuana use, and we could not find a current Oklahoma ruling on whether odor alone justifies a car search.
OK.inPractice: We did not verify how Oklahoma courts treat odor given the state's 2018 medical law and legal hemp. Treat this entry as unconfirmed.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Cannabis in Oklahoma (legal status only)

OR.summary: No. Oregon's Court of Appeals has said that since legalization, the smell of marijuana alone doesn't show you have an illegal amount, so it isn't enough by itself.
OR.inPractice: State v. Robinson, 310 Or. App. 644 (2021), said a strong odor signals marijuana but not necessarily an illegal quantity for adults 21+. Odor can still be weighed with other facts.

sources.label: Marijuana Policy Project / Perkins Coie, 2021 State Analysis Chart (Oregon, discussing State v. Robinson)

PA.summary: No. Pennsylvania's Supreme Court held in 2021 that the smell of marijuana alone can't create probable cause to search a car, though it can be one factor.
PA.inPractice: Commonwealth v. Barr, 266 A.3d 25 (Pa. 2021), relied on the legalization of medical marijuana. Officers need other facts in the totality of the circumstances.

sources.label: Baxter v. State (Fla. 5th DCA 2024), quoting Commonwealth v. Barr, 266 A.3d 25, 41 (Pa. 2021)
State Court Report: legalization and search-and-seizure law (2025)

RI.summary: Unclear. Rhode Island legalized adult use in 2022, and we found no Rhode Island appellate ruling on whether odor alone justifies a car search.
RI.inPractice: A 2021 Superior Court decision (State v. Li) said odor alone isn't enough but can be a factor. Trial-court rulings don't bind other courts.

sources.label: Marijuana Policy Project / Perkins Coie, 2021 State Analysis Chart (Rhode Island)

SC.summary: Probably yes, but unconfirmed. Marijuana isn't legal in South Carolina, and we found nothing showing the state has moved away from treating odor as probable cause.
SC.inPractice: We could not verify a current South Carolina appellate ruling on odor, including whether legal hemp changes it. Treat this entry as unconfirmed.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Legality of cannabis by U.S. jurisdiction (legal status only)

SD.summary: Probably yes, but unconfirmed. Recreational marijuana isn't legal in South Dakota, and we found nothing showing courts have stopped treating odor as probable cause.
SD.inPractice: We could not verify a current South Dakota ruling on odor, or how the 2021 medical law or legal hemp affects it. Treat this entry as unconfirmed.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Legality of cannabis by U.S. jurisdiction (legal status only)

TN.summary: Yes, generally. Tennessee courts have kept upholding searches based on marijuana odor even though legal hemp smells the same.
TN.inPractice: State v. Bishop (Tenn. Crim. App. 2024, unreported) upheld a search despite the officer's admitted inability to tell hemp from marijuana. State v. Green (Tenn. 2024) let a dog's alert count.

sources.label: Bain v. State (Ala. Crim. App. 2024), quoting State v. Bishop (Tenn. Crim. App. 2024)
U.S. Brief in Opposition, Harris v. United States, No. 25-7478 (discussing State v. Green, 697 S.W.3d 634 (Tenn. 2024))

TX.summary: Yes. Texas courts hold that the odor of marijuana alone gives probable cause to search a vehicle, and have rejected the argument that legal hemp changes this.
TX.inPractice: Moulden v. State (Tex. Crim. App. 1978) is a longstanding example; Cortez v. State (Tex. App. 2022, unpublished) applied the rule after hemp legalization.
TX.detail: Not legal; limited low-THC medical program

sources.label: Bain v. State (Ala. Crim. App. 2024), quoting Cortez v. State (Tex. App. 2022)
Marijuana Policy Project / Perkins Coie, 2021 State Analysis Chart (Texas)

UT.summary: Probably yes, but unconfirmed. Recreational marijuana isn't legal in Utah, and we found nothing showing courts have stopped treating odor as probable cause.
UT.inPractice: We could not verify a current Utah ruling on odor, or how the 2018 medical law or legal hemp affects it. Treat this entry as unconfirmed.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Legality of cannabis by U.S. jurisdiction (legal status only)

VT.summary: No. Vermont's Supreme Court held in 2019 that a faint odor of burnt marijuana alone wasn't probable cause to seize and search a car.
VT.inPractice: Zullo v. State (2019 VT 1) treats odor as one factor, not a deciding one. It applied the law after Vermont's 2013 decriminalization; possession became legal in 2018.

sources.label: Marijuana Policy Project / Perkins Coie, 2021 State Analysis Chart (Vermont, discussing Zullo v. State)
WHYY/AP: In era of legal pot, can police search cars based on odor? (2019)

VA.summary: No. Virginia law says police can't stop, search, or seize you based solely on the odor of marijuana, and evidence found in violation is inadmissible, even if you consented.
VA.inPractice: Va. Code § 4.1-1302 (2021). The rule doesn't apply at airports or to commercial motor vehicles.

WA.summary: Unclear. Marijuana is legal for adults in Washington, and we found no appellate ruling since legalization on whether odor alone is probable cause to search a car.
WA.inPractice: The leading case, State v. Grande (2008), predates legalization. After legalization, Seattle police publicly said smell alone wouldn't be a reason to search a vehicle.

sources.label: Marijuana Policy Project / Perkins Coie, 2021 State Analysis Chart (Washington)

WV.summary: Probably yes, but unconfirmed. Recreational marijuana isn't legal in West Virginia, and we found nothing showing courts have stopped treating odor as probable cause.
WV.inPractice: We could not verify a current West Virginia ruling on odor, or how the 2017 medical law or legal hemp affects it. Treat this entry as unconfirmed.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Legality of cannabis by U.S. jurisdiction (legal status only)

WI.summary: Yes, for now. Wisconsin's Supreme Court held in 2023 that a strong marijuana odor linked to the driver can give probable cause to search a car, even though legal CBD smells the same.
WI.inPractice: State v. Moore (2023 WI 50), applying State v. Secrist (1999). In August 2026 the court agreed to hear State v. McAfee on whether odor alone is enough, so this may change.

sources.label: Wisconsin State Public Defender: SCOW grants review in State v. McAfee (Aug. 2026)

WY.summary: Yes. Wyoming's Supreme Court has held that the smell of marijuana establishes probable cause to search a car.
WY.inPractice: Ray v. State (2018 WY 146). We found no later Wyoming ruling on whether legal hemp changes this.

sources.label: Ray v. State, 2018 WY 146
